Men'sWomen's Water Polo Recruiting Board

Where the roster spots are for the high school classes of 2027 through 2030, school by school and position by position, built from every NCAA men'swomen's program's current roster and the commitments reported so far.

Download CSV
How to use this board
  1. Pick Men or Women at the top. Every tab switches with it.
  2. Start with Find my fits: choose a class and position (add an SAT or ACT score if you like) to get a ranked list of programs that are losing players at that position, with an academic read on each.
  3. Click any underlined school name for its profile: admissions numbers, testing policy, aid, NCAA eligibility, returning players by position, commits, feeder clubs and links to the roster, coaching staff and recruiting questionnaire.
  4. The openings tabs show every program's spots by position for 2027 through 2030. Use the Needs filter to see only schools losing players at one position, and click a row for names.
  5. The colored dot next to each player is data confidence: green High (class year from a dated roster or list, several sources), yellow Medium, red Low (class guessed from an age group or a single mention). Open a player to see why, and use Hide low confidence to filter.
  6. The player pool tabs list recruits by class. Click a player for honors and best-fit schools; tap ☆ to build a shortlist, and use My school list on the All schools tab the same way. Both stay in this browser and download from the CSV buttons above.
  7. Feeders & trends shows which clubs and high schools send players where, and which programs are behind last year's pace.
  8. Contacting coaches has guidelines for emailing coaches and a verified directory of every program's coaching staff with email and phone.

Pool who fit counts the uncommitted players on this board in the same class and position who clear the program's bar. Grades: Outstanding Honors (Academic All-American's higher tier) at the Ivies, Stanford, MIT, Caltech, Johns Hopkins, Pomona-Pitzer, Claremont-Mudd-Scripps and the service academies; Academic All-American at other schools admitting 35% or fewer; no grade bar elsewhere, including the top 4 in the poll, where the water polo bar does the filtering. Water polo: a top national record for the top 4 in the poll; a national-level record (selection camp pick, Junior Olympics all-tournament, NISCA All-America, All-CIF Open or Division 1) for other Division I programs; anyone on the board for Division II and III. It's an estimate: test scores aren't public, not every family applies for Academic All-American, international recruits aren't counted, and if you're on the board you're in the count yourself.

How clubs have finished at the two biggest club championships: the Futures Water Polo League Super Finals (each June, California clubs plus invited teams) and USA Water Polo's National Junior Olympics (each July, clubs from across the country; flights from Platinum down to Copper). Each age group plays in tiered divisions (D1 above D2 above D3), so a team's overall place counts every team in the divisions above it. On this board counts players on this board whose listed club is that club (clear name matches only). Sources: futureswpl.com, the league's results sheets and the Kahuna Events results archive.

How water polo players actually pay for college, and the free tools to go after each kind of money. For most families, need-based and merit aid add up to more than athletic money, so a good plan chases all of them at once. Rules and income limits change every year; confirm with each school's financial aid office. Last checked November 2026.

Where the money comes from

  • Athletic scholarships, Division I. Since the 2025 House settlement, Division I schools that opted in have no cap on how many scholarships a sport can give, but every water polo roster is limited to 24 players. A program can now fund more of its roster if the school pays for it; most still split partial scholarships, and full rides go to few players. Ask each coach how their program's money works now.
  • Athletic scholarships, Division II. Partial scholarships split across the roster, usually combined with academic aid.
  • No athletic scholarships: the Ivy League and all of Division III. Harvard, Princeton, Brown, MIT, Caltech, Johns Hopkins, the Claremont colleges and the other Division III programs give only need-based and merit aid. A coach's support still matters a lot, because it helps in admissions.
  • Need-based aid. Based on family income and assets, from the FAFSA and often the CSS Profile. At the wealthiest schools it can beat any athletic offer (see the table below).
  • Merit scholarships. Awarded for grades and test scores, mostly at private schools and Division III; many are automatic at admission. Strong grades also widen the list of schools a coach can get admitted.
  • State aid. California residents can get Cal Grants and the Middle Class Scholarship at California schools; both use the FAFSA or the California Dream Act Application. Priority deadline: March 2, 2027.
  • Out-of-state discount. The Western Undergraduate Exchange (WUE) lets students from western states pay reduced tuition, typically 150% of in-state, at participating public schools such as Hawaii and many Cal State campuses. Each school decides which majors and students qualify.
  • Private scholarships. From foundations, clubs, employers and local groups. Individually small, but they stack.

Tuition-free lines at schools with water polo

SchoolTuition covered when family income is underMore
Princeton$250,000 for most familiesFull cost of attendance covered up to $150,000
Harvard$200,000Families under $100,000 pay nothing
MIT$200,000 (typically)Under $100,000: parents typically pay nothing
Caltech$200,000 (most students)Under $100,000: tuition, fees, housing and food, no loans
Stanford$150,000 (parent income)Under $100,000: no parent contribution expected
BrownNo free-tuition line publishedUnder $60,000: $0 parent contribution for most families

Each line assumes "typical assets," which each school defines differently. Run the school's own net price calculator for your real number. Sources: school financial aid pages, compiled by GradPilot (checked September 2026).

Game plan

  • Freshman and sophomore year. Grades and test scores matter most: they set both merit aid and which schools coaches can get you into. Register with the NCAA Eligibility Center if Division I or II is a possibility.
  • From June 15 after sophomore year. Division I coaches can reply. In those conversations, ask how the program uses scholarship money, how athletic aid combines with academic aid, and what the team's roster size will be.
  • Junior year. Run the net price calculator for every school on your list (each school's profile here shows its cost of attendance and average net price). Ivy League and Division III coaches can ask admissions for an early read on financial aid, called a pre-read; ask whether they offer one.
  • Senior year, from October 1. File the FAFSA (the 2027-28 form is already open for the class of 2027) and the CSS Profile where a school requires it. File early: California and some schools award aid until it runs out.
  • August 1 before senior year onward. Division I and II coaches can put athletic aid offers in writing. Compare offers on total cost after all aid, not the athletic money alone, and ask whether the aid is guaranteed for four years.
  • Apply for outside scholarships all year. Local and water polo scholarships get far fewer applicants than national ones.

Free tools

  • FAFSA (federal and California aid) and the CSS Profile (required by many private schools).
  • Net Price Calculator Center links to every school's calculator; College Navigator shows real costs and aid.
  • California Student Aid Commission: Cal Grant and the Middle Class Scholarship.
  • WUE savings finder: which western public schools offer the discount.
  • Scholarship search: BigFuture Scholarship Search, Fastweb, Scholarships.com, and your high school counselor's local list.
  • Water polo scholarships: USA Water Polo's Justin Dignam Memorial Fund scholarship, and the water polo listings on Scholarships.com and BigFuture. Ask your club too; some clubs and booster groups give their own.
  • NCAA Eligibility Center: required before you can sign with a Division I or II school.

Watch out for

  • Never pay to apply for a scholarship or to "guarantee" one. Legitimate scholarships are free to apply for.
  • Paid recruiting services aren't required. Everything on this page, and contacting coaches yourself, is free.
  • Read the fine print on athletic aid: whether it's renewable, what happens if you're injured or leave the team, and whether it reduces your need-based or merit aid.

How to reach college coaches, and every program's head coach with contact details. Division I coaches can reply from June 15 after sophomore year, but you can write to them before that; they read it and keep notes.

Coaching changes

New head coaches and open searches since last season. A new coach often re-recruits a class, so ask about it if you're talking to one of these programs.

Guidelines

  • Write it yourself. Email from the player's own address, not a parent's, and address the head coach plus the assistant who recruits your area. One school per email, never a group email.
  • Lead with the facts coaches sort by: grad year, position, dominant hand, club and high school, and cap number and color for upcoming events. Put them in the subject line and the first two lines.
  • Say why that school. One specific sentence about the program or academics shows you have done your homework.
  • Keep it short. It should fit on one phone screen. Add height and wingspan, GPA and test scores (or test-optional), honors, your NCAA Eligibility Center ID and your club and high school coaches' contacts.
  • Always send video: a two-to-three-minute highlight reel with your best clips first and yourself marked before each clip, plus one full unedited game with your cap number and color noted. Coaches trust full games more than highlights.
  • Show what your position needs: goals and assists for attackers; drawn ejections and holding position for centers; steals and help defense for defenders; saves, outlets and communication for goalies.
  • Fill out the recruiting questionnaire (linked on each school profile) the same week you email.
  • Follow up around events. Email before Junior Olympics, ODP and big high school tournaments with your schedule and cap, and after with results and new video. Reply to any coach within a day.
  • Keep a log of every school, contact date and reply. The ☆ school list and the CSV download on this board are a good start.

College club water polo: every men'swomen's collegiate club team in the Collegiate Water Polo Association (CWPA), separate from the NCAA varsity programs on the rest of the board. Before June 15 after sophomore year, a Division I coach can send camp information and questionnaires but can't talk recruiting with the player. That is why verbal commitments come in a wave starting in the fall of junior year, and why women's classes, which recruit earlier, fill faster.

Visits

  • Official visits (paid by the school) have been unlimited in number since 2023, but only one per school and no longer than 48 hours. The school can cover travel and meals for the recruit and up to two family members.
  • Unofficial visits (paid by the family) are allowed any time, but meeting with coaches on one follows the Aug 1 before junior year date.

Commitments and signing

  • A verbal commitment is not binding on either side.
  • The National Letter of Intent was eliminated in late 2024. Recruits now sign an athletics aid agreement with the school. Written aid offers can't be made before Aug 1 of senior year, and once a recruit signs, other schools must stop recruiting them.
  • Ivy League schools (Harvard, Princeton, Brown) and Division III schools don't offer athletic scholarships, so a commitment there runs through admissions and need-based aid.

Roster limits and scholarships (House settlement)

Since July 1, 2025, Division I schools that opted into the House settlement no longer have a scholarship cap in water polo (it was 4.5 for men and 8 for women). Instead they have a roster limit of 24 players for both men and women, and they can give aid to any or all of those 24. Players who were already on a roster or already recruited when the rules changed are grandfathered and don't count against the limit.
  • What it means for recruits: schools carrying more than 24 now (shown when you expand a school) will likely sign fewer players than they lose until they're down to 24. Walk-on spots are scarcer than before.
  • Schools that didn't opt in, and Division II and III schools, aren't bound by the 24-player limit.

Transfer portal

  • Division I water polo has one 30-day transfer window a year, starting the day after the NCAA championship field is set. For men that has been early December to early January. For women it has been early May to early June.
  • Transfers can change a school's openings after this board was built, especially at the top programs.

Division II and III

  • Division II: phone calls, off-campus contact and official visits open June 15 after sophomore year. Unofficial visits are allowed any time.
  • Division III: no athletic scholarships. Coaches can call and message any time. Off-campus contact opens after sophomore year and official visits open January 1 of junior year.

Checklist for a recruit

  • Register with the NCAA Eligibility Center (needed for Division I and II) and keep the 16 core courses on track.
  • Fill out each target school's recruiting questionnaire, and send a short highlight video plus a full game along with your club and high school schedules.
  • Coaches watch the Junior Olympics, ODP regionals and nationals, and the top high school tournaments. Make sure your club and high school coaches know your target list.
  • Use the openings tabs to match your position to schools that are actually losing players at it. The Needs filter shows only the schools with an opening at one position.

Sources. NCAA roster limits under the House settlement; June 15 and Aug 1 Division I recruiting dates; unlimited official visits; end of the National Letter of Intent; Division I transfer windows; Division II and III recruiting calendars.

How to read this board, and sources
  • These are the most likely openings, not promised spots. Seniors can take a fifth year, players transfer, and coaches fill some spots with transfers and international players.
  • Schools label positions differently. One program's utility player is another's attacker, so read attack and utility together.
  • Use the Needs filter to see only schools with an opening at one position, ranked by how many. Because schools label positions differently, check attack and utility together.
  • Commit positions come from forum posts; commits whose position wasn't posted reduce a school's total but not a specific position.
  • Women's openings use each school's newest posted roster. Schools that haven't posted their 2026-27 roster yet don't list this fall's freshmen, so their goalie counts can be low.
  • Division I schools that opted into the House settlement are capped at 24 rostered players, with current players grandfathered. UCLA, Air Force, Santa Clara, Navy, Pepperdine, UC Irvine, Brown, Pacific, LMU, UC San Diego and Stanford carry more than 24 now, so their real openings may be smaller than the departures shown. Expand a school to see its roster size.
  • The 24-player Division I limit applies to women too. UCLA, UC Davis, Stanford, La Salle, UC Irvine, Siena, Saint Mary's, Pacific and Iona carry more than 24 now, so their real openings may be smaller than the departures shown.
  • Conferences come from each conference's 2026 preseason poll (MPSF, Big West, WCC, WWPA, GCC, MAAC and the CWPA's NWPC and Mid-Atlantic conferences) plus SCIAC. Several programs change conferences in 2027-28; hover the ⓘ next to the conference filter for details.
  • Academic All-American honors come from USA Water Polo's 2023-24 and 2024-25 lists (a 3.5 GPA or higher). Those lists publish names only, with no club or school, so a player with a very common name could be matched to someone else. The 2025-26 list hasn't been published yet.
  • Division III programs offer no athletic scholarships and carry larger rosters, so their openings are softer than Division I numbers.
  • Not included because their roster pages block automated reading: Penn State Behrend and Austin College.
  • Not included because their roster pages block automated reading or didn't load: Austin College, Penn State Behrend and Cal State LA. Saint Francis (PA) doesn't list most players' positions, so its openings show as position unknown. Princeton, Wagner, Azusa Pacific and Grove City haven't posted 2027 rosters yet, so their numbers use the spring 2026 roster.
